Lesson 01

How do you decide to fine-tune?

Why it matters

Exclude the cheaper fixes with an eval, then train only for the gap that remains.

Try it: Quiz and boss exam

Lesson
01 of 08
Time
8 min
Level
Practice
Decision
Train only after cheaper fixes
Method
LoRA or QLoRA
Evidence
Same tasks, both models

A short answer

I fine-tune only after a fixed task set shows that the schema, the prompt, retrieval, and tools still leave a behavior I can teach with examples. Facts that change stay in retrieval. I keep the adapter only if it beats the base model on that set without new safety failures.

If they ask you to go further

  • Show the scorecard: base versus adapter, regressions named.
  • Say what you refused to train on: secrets, eval rows, data you do not have rights to.
  • Name LoRA or QLoRA as the usual method, and quantization as a different tool.

Check

What do you say if you have not trained a model yet?

Show the answer

Walk the exclusion list on a system you know. 'Not yet, because retrieval was the failure' is a competent answer.

Lesson 02

How do you evaluate a prompt or model change?

Why it matters

Same tasks, four numbers, a gate you wrote beforehand.

Try it: Quiz and boss exam

Lesson
02 of 08
Time
8 min
Level
Practice
Same
Tasks
Four
Quality, safety, latency, cost
Written
Before you look

A short answer

I keep a versioned task set and score quality, safety, latency, and cost. I pin the prompt, model id, and index. I compare to the last baseline and block the change if a safety task regresses or the gate I wrote in advance fails.

If they ask you to go further

  • Separate retrieval recall from answer quality.
  • Use exact checks where you can, and a rubric-backed judge only where you must, audited by hand.
  • Do not hide a regression inside a flat average.

Check

What is a regression?

Show the answer

A task that passed on the baseline and fails on the change.

Lesson 03

How do you stop an agent from doing damage?

Why it matters

An allowlist, a step cap, validated arguments, and a person on side effects.

Try it: Quiz and boss exam

Lesson
03 of 08
Time
8 min
Level
Practice
List
Allowlist
Cap
Steps and spend
Person
Side effects

A short answer

The agent can call only named tools. Arguments have to match the schema before the handler runs. Read-only tools stay inside a step and spend cap. Sending, paying, deleting, and pushing wait for a person who sees the exact arguments. The trace is what I review, not the summary.

If they ask you to go further

  • Approval is a record in your program, not a field the model sets.
  • Retries of side effects need idempotency keys.
  • Tool descriptions are untrusted text.

Check

Why not rely on the system prompt?

Show the answer

Because a document the model reads can contradict it, and a tool that is wired up can still be called.

Lesson 04

What is MCP, and when would you use it?

Why it matters

A protocol for connecting a host to a tool server, when more than one app should share that server.

Try it: Quiz and boss exam

Lesson
04 of 08
Time
8 min
Level
Practice
What
A protocol, not a model
When
More than one app shares a server
Unless
You have not read the server

A short answer

MCP lets a host's client talk to a server that exposes tools, resources, and prompts over stdio locally or HTTP remotely. I use it when I want a reviewed server — notes, tickets, docs — available to an assistant without inventing a plugin format. I do not enable a server I have not read, and I do not auto-approve write tools.

If they ask you to go further

  • Host, client, and server are different roles. The server is not the model.
  • Resources are still untrusted input.
  • A remote server needs authentication and least privilege.

Check

Is installing an MCP server free?

Show the answer

No. It is a permission change. Treat it like a plugin.

Lesson 05

How do you review a coding agent's change?

Why it matters

Read the diff, rerun the tests, and reject hunks that do not serve the goal.

Try it: Quiz and boss exam

Lesson
05 of 08
Time
8 min
Level
Practice
Read
The diff
Rerun
The tests
Reject
Hunks that miss the goal

A short answer

I look at the diff as a teammate's change: extra files, weakened tests, new dependencies, and anything outside the goal. I run the test command myself and read the output. Secrets, push, and unrestricted shell are denied in the tool layer. The person who merges is responsible.

If they ask you to go further

  • A plan before a wide edit is cheaper than unwinding one.
  • A test the agent rewrote to go green is a failed review.
  • Lines generated is not the metric. Review time and escaped bugs are.

Check

The agent says tests passed. What do you need to see?

Show the answer

The command and the output, rerun by you, plus a test diff that still asserts the behavior you wanted.

Lesson 06

How do you control cost and latency?

Why it matters

Smaller context, a cheaper model where the eval allows it, caps, and cost per successful task.

Try it: Quiz and boss exam

Lesson
06 of 08
Time
7 min
Level
Practice
Context
Smaller
Model
Cheaper where the eval allows
Unit
Cost per successful task

A short answer

I retrieve passages instead of pasting the corpus, cap output tokens, and route easy rows to a smaller model only when those rows pass the same checks. I set timeouts and backoff. I report cost per successful task, not per call, and I read the provider's current prices rather than a memorized rate.

If they ask you to go further

  • Prompt caching and batch are levers when the workload matches them. Measure the cache hit.
  • A reasoning model is a latency decision, not a default.
  • A retry storm is a design bug.

Check

Why not cost per call?

Show the answer

Retries, failures, and human cleanup are part of the cost of one success.

Lesson 07

How do you know a grounded answer is not invented?

Why it matters

The citation has to be an id you retrieved, and some tasks must refuse.

Try it: Quiz and boss exam

Lesson
07 of 08
Time
7 min
Level
Practice
Cite
An id you retrieved
Refuse
When it is absent
Ignore
A tone of certainty

A short answer

I score retrieval separately: did the right chunk id appear. The answer may cite only ids that were retrieved, and the code drops the rest. The task set includes questions the corpus cannot answer, where refusal is the pass. A fluent paragraph with a made-up bibliography fails.

If they ask you to go further

  • Hybrid search plus a reranker is the usual pipeline.
  • If recall is bad, I do not tune the writing prompt first.
  • I store the index time next to the source time.

Check

What do you check in code, not by reading tone?

Show the answer

That every cited id was in the retrieved set, and that a refusal task did not invent one.

Lesson 08

What goes in an AI product spec?

Why it matters

The job, the non-goals, the four numbers, the failure states, and the kill switch.

Try it: Quiz and boss exam

Lesson
08 of 08
Time
8 min
Level
Practice
Has
Job, non-goals, four numbers
Also
Failure states
And
A kill switch

A short answer

I write the person's job before the model name, including what this version will not do. Success is quality, safety, latency, and cost per successful task, plus a counter-metric so the team cannot game one number. Empty, slow, wrong, and unsafe states are specified. A limited release has an audience and a way to turn the model path off.

If they ask you to go further

  • Buying an agent UI does not replace the eval or the data policy.
  • Voice adds a latency budget, a transcript, and a human handoff.
  • Unattended send is a non-goal unless someone has owned that risk in writing.

Check

Why name non-goals?

Show the answer

An unnamed non-goal gets built the moment a demo suggests it.
